title: Conflict-of-Interest Check
description: Hash-map-of-sets adjacency lookup — build a Map of adverse-party -> matter-ids and a Set of our own clients from existing matters in one pass, then check a prospective client against both indexes in O(1).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down what counts as a conflict and what the output should look like.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: we represent plaintiffs against defendants. Given a list of existing matters (each with `id`, `plaintiff`, `defendants[]`) and a prospective client name, I need to flag a conflict if the prospect is either (a) an adverse party in any matter — they're a defendant we've opposed — or (b) already a current client (a plaintiff we represent). Clarifying questions:"

• Are names matched exactly (case-sensitive) or normalized (case-insensitive, trimmed)? Real-world data has spelling variants.
• Can one prospect hit BOTH conflict types — adverse in one matter AND a current client in another? Do I report both reasons or just the most severe?
• Closed/inactive matters — do they still count, or only active ones? (Conflict rules in most jurisdictions: yes, closed matters still conflict.)
• Output — single string per prospect, or structured data for the UI to format? And what's the exact phrasing the downstream system expects?
sections.why: The 'both conflict types at once' question is the structural one — it decides whether we return on the first match or collect all reasons into an array. The product answer is almost always 'collect all', because a conflict report that hides reasons is worse than one that over-reports. The case-sensitivity question is the lawyer's-data question: in production this is where 90% of bugs come from, and asking signals you've handled name-matching before.

sections.title: 2. Spot the shape
sections.prompt: What's the data structure pattern that makes this O(1) per prospect?
sections.say:
"This is a build-index-once, query-many problem — same shape as Two Sum or any hash-map adjacency lookup. Two indexes:"

• `adverse`: a Map from defendant-name → array of matter ids where they're a defendant. Map, not Set, because one party can be a defendant across multiple matters and the report has to name each matter.
• `ourClients`: a Set of plaintiff names. Just membership — we don't need to list matters here, only whether they're a client.

"One pass over the matters to build both indexes. Then each prospect check is O(1) for the Set lookup plus O(k) to list the k matters they're adverse in. If we have m matters with average d defendants and q prospects to check, total cost is O(m·d + q) — way better than the O(m·d·q) brute force of rescanning matters per prospect."
sections.why: Naming the two indexes AND defending why one is a Map of arrays and the other is a Set is the load-bearing move. The naïve answer is 'use a Set for both', which loses the matter ids and forces a second scan to recover them. The build-once/query-many framing also matters because it's exactly how this would deploy in production — a batch-loaded index that handles thousands of intake queries per day, not a function called once per matter set.

sections.title: 3. Walk a tiny example
sections.prompt: Trace one input end-to-end to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me run two matters and three prospects through the model."

examples.input: matters=[{id:'M-1', plaintiff:'Acme', defendants:['Globex','Initech']}, {id:'M-2', plaintiff:'Wayne', defendants:['Globex']}], prospects=['Globex','Stark','Acme']
examples.output: Globex: CONFLICT — adverse party in M-1; adverse party in M-2\nStark: CLEAR\nAcme: CONFLICT — already a current client
examples.note: Globex is adverse in both matters; Acme is a current plaintiff; Stark is clean.
examples.trace:
Build phase:
  M-1: ourClients += Acme; adverse[Globex]=[M-1]; adverse[Initech]=[M-1]
  M-2: ourClients += Wayne; adverse[Globex]=[M-1, M-2]
Query phase:
  'Globex': adverse hit → reasons=['adverse party in M-1', 'adverse party in M-2']; ourClients miss
    → 'Globex: CONFLICT — adverse party in M-1; adverse party in M-2'
  'Stark': adverse miss; ourClients miss → 'Stark: CLEAR'
  'Acme': adverse miss; ourClients hit → reasons=['already a current client']
    → 'Acme: CONFLICT — already a current client'

sections.why: The Globex case is the one to trace — it shows why the Map stores an array, not a single id. If we stored only the last matter (overwrite on collision) the report would say 'adverse party in M-2' and silently drop M-1. The Acme case earns its keep because it proves the ourClients Set check fires independently of the adverse check; without it, Acme would read as CLEAR even though we already represent them.

sections.title: 4. Edge cases & failure modes
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Partial-match conflicts — 'Globex Corp' vs 'Globex' or 'globex' vs 'Globex'. Exact-match misses real conflicts. In production you'd want a normalization layer (lowercase + trim + maybe fuzzy match) BEFORE the index lookup. Flag this but don't build it unless asked.
• Empty `matters` array — both indexes are empty Maps; every prospect returns CLEAR. Works by construction.
• Prospect is BOTH adverse and a current client — we collect both reasons into `conflicts[]` and join them with `'; '`. The output reads `CONFLICT — adverse party in M-3; already a current client`.
• Same defendant listed twice in one matter — would push the matter id twice. Worth deduping with a Set, but the duplicate-list bug is usually upstream (in the matter intake) so a defensive check here masks it.
• Em-dash vs hyphen — the format string uses U+2014 (—), not the regular hyphen-minus (-). Eyeballing the source file won't tell them apart; the exact-match output comparison will. This is a real gotcha for anyone copying the format string by hand.
• Case sensitivity — `Acme` ≠ `acme`. Same as the partial-match problem: solve in a normalization layer, not inside the conflict check.
sections.why: The em-dash gotcha is the iteration-killer if you're authoring the lesson — the validator's exact-string comparison won't tell you 'wrong character', just 'output mismatch', and you'll stare at the file for ten minutes. Calling that out unprompted shows you've debugged this kind of thing before. The normalization-layer answer to case/partial matching is the senior-tier signal: you're refusing to put fuzzy logic inside what should be a pure index lookup.

sections.title: 5. Complexity & memory
sections.prompt: How would you defend the bounds?
sections.say:
"Build time is O(m · d̄) where m is the number of matters and d̄ is the average number of defendants per matter — one pass over matters, one inner pass over each defendant list, two Map/Set writes per inner step (each O(1) amortized).

Query time per prospect is O(1) for the two membership checks plus O(k) to enumerate the matter ids the prospect appears in. For most prospects k is 0 or small.

Space is O(m · d̄) for the `adverse` Map (one entry per (matter, defendant) pair) plus O(m) for the `ourClients` Set (one per matter's plaintiff). Total memory scales linearly with the input.

The interesting tradeoff: if we never query more than once, we could skip the index and do an O(m · d̄) linear scan per prospect — same cost, simpler. But conflict checking is canonically a batch operation (running intake reports nightly, or checking a list of prospects against the book of business), so the index pays for itself the second time."
sections.why: Naming the build-vs-query tradeoff explicitly is the senior signal — it shows you'd choose the simpler linear scan if the use case were truly one-shot, instead of reflexively pre-indexing because 'maps are O(1)'. Most candidates skip the tradeoff and over-engineer. The 'one entry per (matter, defendant) pair' framing also makes the space bound concrete instead of hand-wavy.

sections.title: 6. Robustness & tests
sections.prompt: What would you write to lock this in?
sections.say:
"Test cases I'd want before shipping:"

• Adverse-only conflict — single matter, prospect is a defendant. Should return one reason, naming the matter id.
• Client-only conflict — prospect is a plaintiff. Should return `'already a current client'`.
• Adverse-across-multiple-matters — proves the Map-of-arrays handles list growth correctly. Both matter ids in the reason list.
• Both reasons at once — prospect is adverse in one matter AND a current client in another. Both reasons surface, joined with `'; '`.
• Clean prospect — no conflict found, returns the `CLEAR` string. The negative test.
• Empty matters — every prospect is CLEAR. Lock down the empty-init case.
• Em-dash regression — assert the exact byte sequence in the CONFLICT output, not a substring match.

"Beyond tests: in production this would log every CONFLICT result for compliance, and the index would be rebuilt incrementally as matters are opened/closed, not from scratch on every query. Those are layers around the kernel, but the kernel — the two-index lookup — stays the same."
sections.why: The em-dash regression test is the unsexy-but-load-bearing one — it locks down the format string against accidental edits where someone retypes the dash and breaks every downstream comparison. The incremental-index note at the end shows you see this as a service-shaped problem (built once at startup, mutated as state changes) rather than a one-call function. That's the production framing the interviewer wants to hear.

trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter checkConflict — matters=${matters.length}, prospect='${prospect}'`, state: { matters, prospect, adverse: [], ourClients: [] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `M='${m.id}' — add plaintiff '${m.plaintiff}' to ourClients`, state: { mId: m.id, plaintiff: m.plaintiff, adverse: [...adverse.entries()], ourClients: [...ourClients] } };

yield { line: 8, label: `M='${m.id}' — index defendant '${def}' → adverse[${def}]=[${adverse.get(def).join(',')}]`, state: { mId: m.id, def, adverse: [...adverse.entries()].map(([k, v]) => [k, [...v]]), ourClients: [...ourClients] } };

yield { line: 11, label: `indexes built — query prospect '${prospect}'`, state: { prospect, adverse: [...adverse.entries()].map(([k, v]) => [k, [...v]]), ourClients: [...ourClients], conflicts: [] } };
yield { line: 13, label: `adverse hit '${prospect}' in '${id}' → push reason`, state: { prospect, id, conflicts: [...conflicts] } };
yield { line: 13, label: `adverse miss for '${prospect}'`, state: { prospect, conflicts: [...conflicts] } };
yield { line: 15, label: `ourClients hit '${prospect}' → push 'already a current client'`, state: { prospect, conflicts: [...conflicts] } };
yield { line: 15, label: `ourClients miss for '${prospect}'`, state: { prospect, conflicts: [...conflicts] } };
yield { line: 18, label: `return '${result}'`, state: { prospect, conflicts: [...conflicts], returns: result } };

notes: Index defendant -> [matter ids] in a Map, because one party can be a defendant across multiple matters. A plain Set of defendant names would lose which matters they appear in.
Track our own plaintiffs in a separate Set too: we cannot represent someone we are already adverse to, AND we should not double-represent an existing client, so both indexes are checked.
The output uses a literal em-dash character (—, U+2014), not a hyphen-minus. The expected output will not match if you type a regular '-'.
Time O(m·d̄ + q·k) build + query — m matters, d̄ avg defendants/matter to build indexes; q prospects each O(1) membership check + O(k) to list k adverse matter ids. Space O(m·d̄).

questions.q: Why index defendants as a Map of name -> array-of-matter-ids rather than a plain Set of defendant names?
options: A Set's `has()` is O(n); a Map's `has()` is O(1), so the conflict check must use Map
One party can be a defendant across multiple matters, and we need to report which matter ids they appear in
Set deduplicates entries silently, so two matters with the same defendant would be collapsed into one
Iterating a Set is non-deterministic, so the matter-id list would come out in a different order each call
questions.explain: A Set would tell you only that someone is adverse, not in which matters. The Map preserves the matter ids so the conflict report can name them.

questions.q: Why does the function also track our own plaintiffs in a separate Set?
options: To filter the prospect out of the `adverse` index before reporting
We cannot represent both sides, so a prospect who is already our client is also a conflict — a different reason than being adverse
Plaintiffs are stored in `adverse` too, so the Set deduplicates them on output
So the rebuild logic can re-derive plaintiffs without re-scanning every matter's defendant list
questions.explain: Two distinct conflict reasons: the prospect is on the other side of a matter (adverse), or we already represent them (current client). Both must be checked.

questions.q: The CONFLICT output joins reasons with a special character. Which is it?
questions.explain: The format string uses a literal em-dash (—). Typing a plain hyphen would make the output fail an exact-match comparison.

questions.q: What is the lookup cost of checking a single prospect after the indexes are built?
options: O(1) for the membership checks, plus O(k) to list the k matters they're adverse in
O(n^2) for the nested defendant loop
questions.explain: Map/Set membership is constant time; the only extra work is iterating the (usually small) list of matter ids the prospect appears in.

L3.prompt: We represent plaintiffs against defendants. Given existing matters ({id, plaintiff, defendants[]}) and a prospective client name, flag a conflict if the prospect is an adverse party (a defendant) in any matter — list those matter ids — or is already a current client. Otherwise CLEAR. Print the result for an adverse party, a clear name, and an existing client.
L3.expectedOutput:
Globex: CONFLICT — adverse party in M-1; adverse party in M-2
Stark Inc: CLEAR
Acme Corp: CONFLICT — already a current client
hints: First pass: build a Map of defendant -> [matter ids] and a Set of plaintiff names from the matters.
Collect conflict reasons into an array: one 'adverse party in <id>' per matter the prospect is a defendant in, plus 'already a current client' if they're a plaintiff.
If no reasons, return '<name>: CLEAR'; otherwise join the reasons with '; ' after a literal em-dash (—).
